commentary.bottom_line: Five studies test interpretable or explainable approaches, and three report accuracy that matched or exceeded a comparison, but none measures whether clinicians understand or check AI decisions better. The evidence comes from offline benchmarks and one uncontrolled pre-post deployment, so certainty is very low.

perspectives.view: Four of five studies are offline or benchmark evaluations, and the one real deployment lacks a comparator. Three studies measure model accuracy, one describes output structure, and one tests post-hoc explanation methods. None measures clinician understanding, error detection, or patient outcomes. Indirectness and risk of bias lower certainty to very low. The endorsing sources are mostly commentaries and one framework.

In one deployment, a rule-based triage pipeline raised emergency recall from 0.565 to 0.810, which suggests fewer missed emergencies, though the study had no concurrent control. An ECG benchmark found that LIME, KernelShap, and LRP failed to highlight clinically meaningful features. This finding suggests that some post-hoc explanations of black-box models may mislead users.

Auditable shape functions exposed non-linear thresholds and interactions for age, smoking, income, and diabetes. A chest X-ray model made every prediction decomposable into concept contributions. No study tested whether clinicians used these outputs in real workflows, how much time they took, or whether the outputs changed decisions.

A sparse BagNet performed on par with a comparable black-box model and generalised to external data. A concept-decomposable chest X-ray model reported state-of-the-art performance on four external datasets, although its abstract gives no numbers. These results suggest the accuracy cost of interpretable models may be small. No study reports development, validation, or maintenance costs.

The United States survey analysis used income as a model variable but did not report performance by income, insurance, language, or literacy group. The Indian triage deployment did not describe patient language or literacy. None of the five studies reports subgroup results for underserved populations.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares interpretable and black-box models on whether clinicians detect model errors, how accurate their decisions are, how long decisions take, or how patients fare in live care. Controlled deployment studies are needed, including in United States safety-net settings, with subgroup reporting by insurance, language, and literacy.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the five tests reported results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The United States survey data included income only as a predictor, and the Indian deployment did not describe language or literacy. Whether interpretable models help clinicians who serve these populations remains untested.
